> Date: Tue, 17 Nov 2026 05:16:43 +0000
> 
> "Dr. Arne Babenhauserheide" <arne_bab@web.de> writes:
> 
> > See GPL 3.0 point 1: https://www.gnu.org/licenses/gpl-3.0
> > »The “source code” for a work means the preferred form of the work for
> > making modifications to it.«
> >
> > That’s why what matters is not just what’s possible, but what’s intended.
> 
> There is a jump in your reasoning here, which I do not get.  First of
> all, I think that if you want to make changes to vibe-spell as such, it
> is just outright preferred to edit the Elisp code

Why is it preferable?  If the baseline is the C++ code of Nuspell,
starting from that would be my first choice, since it avoids the need
to manually look for the ELisp code corresponding to each and every
change in C++.  Don't you agree?

> secondly we have to
> keep in mind that GPLv3 was not written in consideration of the
> possibility that you could have multiple equally preferable source texts
> that you can automatically translate from one to the other and vice
> versa -- of at least I cannot think of an example where you would have a
> (trans-)compilation where the output of such a process would be human
> editable and back-translatable by automatic means as well.

I don't see "multiple equally preferable source texts" here, FWIW,
because what we have is the original C++ code which was translated
into ELisp.  The relation between them is not symmetrical.

> > And how I read it, the preferred way to backport changes from hunspell
> > is to pipe diffs to hunspell C++ source through a proprietary LLM as
> > part of letting the LLM change the source of vibe-spell until it likely
> > matches the change in hunspell.
> 
> First of all, this is all under the hypothetical that Augusto wants to
> backport changes.

That's not our only worry.  Free Software is about allowing _anyone_
to rebuild the program, with or without changes.  And that obviously
includes the use case of following the upstream Nuspell changes,
because someone might want to do that.

This is why we always prefer to consider the original source as the
"preferred form".  One immediate example is the Org source of the Org
manual: we decided not to treat the generated Texinfo as the source,
but provide the full Org code as the source.

> 
> The man page of git-subtree says this
> 
>   Tip
> 
>   In order to keep your commit messages clean, we recommend that
>   people split their commits between the subtrees and the main project
>   as much as possible. That is, if you make a change that affects both
>   the library and the main application, commit it in two pieces. That
>   way, when you split the library commits out later, their
>   descriptions will still make sense. But if this isn’t important to
>   you, it’s not necessary. git subtree will simply leave out the
>   non-library-related parts of the commit when it splits it out into
>   the subproject later.

I wasn't aware that we are treating MPS as a Git subtree.  I thought
we completely imported MPS into our Git repository.  Am I mistaken?

> So I think the commit history will be nicer if commits MPS and Emacs are
> not intermixed.  And currently "git log mps" looks pretty good to me.

In most cases I'd expect that to look clean even without the
restriction.  It is a rare occasion that would need changes both in
and outside of MPS, but that could well happen.  For example, imagine
that the changes I installed are not enough, and we will need a more
strict synchronization between MPS and Emacs to avoid two threads
suspending each other (e.g., maybe we will need a mutex).  In such
cases, it makes very little sense to separate changes in two files if
they use the same mutex.

Anyway, I'm fine with keeping this for now, but let's please document
this in admin/notes/git-workflow, because people will not expect to be
unable to commit changes like I tried, and will be surprised (and the
error message is not very self-explanatory).  And then let's see what
others think about this restriction when they bump into it.

Hi Philip,

Philip Kaludercic <philipk@posteo.net> writes:

> No problem, but was the code LLM generated then? If so, you 
> should
> annotate it.

No, it was not. Choosing NonGNU ELPA was solely to keep things 
simple
and avoid the copyright assignment paperwork for now, but maybe in 
the
future.

> OK, and not knowing much about this stuff, can you explain why 
> you are
> preforming these computations in the physical color space as 
> opposed
> to a perceptual color space like Oklab?

In au-themes the luminance is only used to tell light themes from
dark ones (comparing bg-main with fg-main) and to show Y in the
annotation, so a perceptual space would not change anything there.

The contrast checks in the test suite need luminance as well, 
because
both WCAG 2 and APCA define contrast on luminance, so I have to 
compute
it as the standards do. Where the question is "do these two 
colours look
different", the tests use perceptual spaces instead: OKLab/OKLCh 
for hue
and lightness steps between syntax roles, and CIEDE2000 for colour
difference at glyph size.

> That sounds useful, please do that!

Two typos are now bug#82264.
(https://lists.gnu.org/archive/html/bug-gnu-emacs/2026-11/msg00877.html)
I will send the patch that adds public functions to color.el 
separately.

> I do not understand, isn't that the current state you are 
> describing,
> or what are you trying to say?

Yeah, that was unclear, my bad. Yes, it is the current state; I 
was
describing how I fixed the behaviour you pointed out (the theme 
stayed
applied after the input was changed).

> OK, but I didn't say anything about these things, my point was 
> really
> just that I wouldn't re-implement the consult feature of 
> changing
> themes according to the current state of the minibuffer.

I understand, but I would like to keep the preview. For the people 
these
themes are made for, the useful way to choose is to see the 
candidate on
their own buffers before committing to it. Without consult there 
would
be no preview at all. With consult I now just call consult-theme, 
so
nothing is re-implemented there. The fallback is about 30 lines, 
uses
only minibuffer-with-setup-hook and a buffer-local 
post-command-hook,
and leaves the completion UI alone. If you still think it is too 
much, I
could put it behind a user option.

Thanks,
Szymon

Eli Zaretskii [17/Nov  3:17pm +02] wrote:
>> The man page of git-subtree says this
>>
>>   Tip
>>
>>   In order to keep your commit messages clean, we recommend that
>>   people split their commits between the subtrees and the main project
>>   as much as possible. That is, if you make a change that affects both
>>   the library and the main application, commit it in two pieces. That
>>   way, when you split the library commits out later, their
>>   descriptions will still make sense. But if this isn=E2=80=99t importan=
t to
>>   you, it=E2=80=99s not necessary. git subtree will simply leave out the
>>   non-library-related parts of the commit when it splits it out into
>>   the subproject later.
>
> I wasn't aware that we are treating MPS as a Git subtree.  I thought
> we completely imported MPS into our Git repository.  Am I mistaken?

There isn't a distinction between a Git subtree and performing a
complete import of something.  This is one of the nice properties of Git
subtrees.

On balance it seems to me wise to follow the git-subtree man page's
advice here.

Sean Whitton

> declaring GPL compliance.  Which will make this requirement an
> integral part of the job to add FFI to Emacs.
>
> Not sure what makes more sense.

I think your second suggestion makes more sense: If someone wants to
work on it, she/he knows right away about that requirement.

Personal note: I presume this point was discussed thoroughly as the
decision was made, and I'm not familiar enough with how FFI's in general
work, but to me, the requirement sounds like: The Lisp interpreter
should recognize if the user is loading a lisp-library which talks to a
non-free, SaaS LLM, so Emacs should block that library.  I fail to see
why Emacs shouldn't support a free library like libffi (Expat License),
and then give users the freedom to decide how to use that interface.

Not sure if that decision should be reconsidered from a different POV,
someday.

P.S.: I do hope this one opinion doesn't produce large volume of mails
and discussions in this group.

Best, Arash

> and then give users the freedom to decide how to use that interface.

Because FFI is not used to perform some stand-alone functionality, it
is used to directly interface Lisp with any arbitrary library.  The
module interface was invented as a replacement, and it requires the
library to declare GPL compatibility, but otherwise can do whatever
FFI can do, albeit less easily, perhaps.

> Not sure if that decision should be reconsidered from a different POV,
> someday.

Feel free to raise this with RMS, but I personally don't see what POV
could significantly affect the decision.

Robert Pluim <rpluim@gmail.com> writes:

>>>>>> On Tue, 17 Nov 2026 13:43:27 +0100, Nickolai Dobrynin

>
>     Nickolai> Oops, that's a bug. And it is my bug. It wasn't there
>     before. I will
>     Nickolai> send in a fix and change "length" to "string-bytes", as
>     you mentioned.

> OK.

How is this for a solution? (See attached).

Also, since we are having this discussion, another quirk from the past
is that a non-ASCII query string is sent out verbatim, e.g.

288 UID SEARCH TEXT "����"

when neither LITERAL+ nor UTF8-NATIVE is available. (!) I did not change
this behavior, even through it's practically guaranteed to fail. That's
also why Gmail search broke down after Google stopped offering LITERAL+,
allegedly for security reasons.

Yet another quirk is a lack of consistency between the way double quotes
are treated. When the string is sent as a binary literal, the IMAP
server seems to treat the quotes as part of the string, but not if the
same string is sent in quotes as in the example above. It's, obviously,
up to the client to reconcile the two.

All in all, we will never get tired going down this IMAP rabbit hole.

>From 6a66f2b2e2fb23a30e54c443404df04377f362ab Mon Sep 17 00:00:00 2001
From: Nickolai Dobrynin <ndobrynin@gmail.com>
Date: Tue, 17 Nov 2026 21:41:31 +0100
Subject: [PATCH] IMAP search: do not double-quote query strings.

This is a follow-up to 6ffa3a5bc738306cfcaed28784f8fcdac49773dc.
* lisp/gnus/gnus-search.el (gnus-search-imap-handle-string):
re-factored and simplified.
---
 lisp/gnus/gnus-search.el | 26 ++++++++++++--------------
 1 file changed, 12 insertions(+), 14 deletions(-)

diff --git a/lisp/gnus/gnus-search.el b/lisp/gnus/gnus-search.el
index c7bf75359fa..0753d36e085 100644
--- a/lisp/gnus/gnus-search.el
+++ b/lisp/gnus/gnus-search.el
@@ -1361,20 +1361,18 @@ gnus-search-imap-handle-string
     ;; do not accept any CHARSET but US-ASCII, but they do report
     ;; Literal+ capability.  So what do we do?  Will quoted strings
     ;; always work?
-    (if (string-match-p "[^[:ascii:]]" str)
-	;; If LITERAL+ is available and native UTF-8 isn't,
-	;; use LITERAL+ and encode `str' as UTF-8.
-	(if (and literal-plus (not utf8-native))
-            (let ((ub-str (encode-coding-string str 'utf-8)))
-              (format "{%d+}\n%s" (length ub-str) ub-str))
-	  ;; Otherwise, if the user hasn't already quoted the string,
-	  ;; quote it for them.
-	  (if (string-prefix-p "\"" str)
-	      str
-	    (format "\"%s\"" str)))
-      (if utf8-native
-          (format "\"%s\"" str)
-        str))))
+    (if (or
+         utf8-native
+         (not (string-match-p "[^[:ascii:]]" str))
+         (not literal-plus))
+        ;; Quote the `str' if the user hasn't:
+        (if (and
+             (string-prefix-p "\"" str)
+             (string-suffix-p "\"" str))
+            str
+          (format "\"%s\"" str))
+      (let ((ub-str (encode-coding-string str 'utf-8)))
+        (format "{%d+}\n%s" (string-bytes ub-str) ub-str)))))
 
 (defun gnus-search-imap-handle-flag (flag)
   "Adjust string FLAG to help IMAP recognize it.

> compute

> look
> different", the tests use perceptual spaces instead: OKLab/OKLCh for
> hue
> and lightness steps between syntax roles, and CIEDE2000 for colour
> difference at glyph size.

> On Wed, 11 Nov 2026, Augusto Stoffel wrote:
>
>> (From the other subthread.)
>>
>> On Tue, 10 Nov 2026, Philip Kaludercic wrote:
>>
>>> To open a can of worms at the end, it might not be a bad idea to use a
>>> different name for the package.  My hunch is that some of the attention
>>> this thread has attracted is due to the name that has a negative
>>> connotation.  The approach to spelling is sound after all, it is not
>>> just a "vibe-check".  What do you think of "espell"?
>>
>> Here I would appreciate the opinion from Arne and the others with
>> concerns about LLM-generated code.  Do you think I should rename the
>> package?
>>
>> I named it that way 1. as an attempt to be a bit funny, in a
>> self-deprecating way, and 2. to not let anybody have the wrong idea
>> about the method used to write that large (but not unreasonable large)
>> amount of code.  I certainly didn't mean to be provocative.
>
> I haven't heard from any of the people I thought I would be benefiting
> by making the nature of the code generation clear from the package name.
>
> I could take the name espell.  If namespaces wee auctioned this one
> would have a high price...  So I could also leave that name for a
> morally purer implementation and take vspell, which at that point would
> be just a random identifier.

It is really up to you in the end, I think all the suggestions are fine,
it would be nice to hear some more opinions... a good old "how to name
this package" discussion would be a nice change of pace.

>> (I don't want to expound on my opinion about LLMs here, but I have fun
>> in actually writing ELisp and I'm not on the Emacs payroll or following
>> deadlines, so this package to me is a rather special experiment.  All my
>> other packages are and will remain handcrafted.)
>
> By the way, we should perhaps have a more precise way to tag packages as
> LLM-assisted.  I for one do have my reservations and would appreciate
> something on those lines.

The MELPA people suggest using an "Assisted-by" pseudo-header, see
https://yhetil.org/emacs-devel/8733w7bipe.fsf@bernoul.li/.  They
explicitly annotate what LLM was used, but I don't know if that is
reasonable as IIUC some people use a whole combination of different
models, or some (like you mentioned) don't see why they should advertise
their services.  For most SaaSS providers the information isn't that
useful after all for some weak notion of reproducability, since they can
just revoke availability of the model.  The long term solution is to add
this to the list of thing that an updated ELPA protocol would formally
declare about a package.

[[[ To any NSA and FBI agents reading my email: please consider    ]]]
[[[ whether defending the US Constitution against all enemies,     ]]]
[[[ foreign or domestic, requires you to follow Snowden's example. ]]]

  > > "Dr. Arne Babenhauserheide" <arne_bab@web.de> writes:
  > >> I expected everyone to see the contradiction of both "modify by hand"
  > >> and "point LLM to hunspell sources to backport".

Philip Kaludercic <philipk@posteo.net> writes:

  > > Please explain, because I see no contradiction here.  You can make
  > > changes by hand, you can make changes using an LLM.  It will be faster
  > > if you do the latter, but that doesn't mean the former isn't possible?

(Someone mentioned a program called Nuspell, but I don't know
what that is or how it relates.  As far as I recall, vibe-spell is
an LLM translation of Hunspell.)

If it is clearly tempting to use an LLM to port changes in Hunspell
into vibe-spell, we cannot sensibly treat vibe-spell as independent
source code.  We would betray our goal if we installed code whose
maintenance depends on a nonfree program or SaaSS server.

That would also add to the general pressure to yield to LLMs.  We will
certainly face such general pressure, as people who don't feel concern
about this issue try to insist we become dependent on LLMs.  We will
face a struggle to refuse.  It would be foolish to choose to make that
struggle harder.

I am convinced that one requirement for including LLM-generated
material in GNU Programs must be that the LLM-generated material be
completely divorced from the LLM that generated it.  In other words,
we must insist there be no reason to anticipate pressure to use LLMs
to update it.  It must be source code, pure and simple, to be
maintained like the rest of Emacs.

In particular, LLM output should not be a machine translation of a
source for which we expect further development.

[[[ To any NSA and FBI agents reading my email: please consider    ]]]
[[[ whether defending the US Constitution against all enemies,     ]]]
[[[ foreign or domestic, requires you to follow Snowden's example. ]]]

  > Yes, so to specialize the claim here, the question is does the usage
  > of LLMs in the translation of this package constitute an action that
  > has consequences that affect other developers in a way that would
  > require these to use proprietary software or some SaaSS?

It can.  There are several ways it could.

1. It could bring in copyright infringement and we might have to
remove that file.

2. It could create a situation where we face temptation, even pressure,
to continue development of that program with LLMs, thus becoming
a permanent dependence on LLMs.

  > For me the most reasonable objection would be the 3k lines of code
  > (~140K).  Yet I argue it cannot be the size of the package that
  > matters, for otherwise just in NonGNU ELPA we would also have the
  > reject the following packages that have at least the same file size as
  > vibe-spell:

You are trying to argue by reductio ad absurdam, but you haven't stated
what position you are arguing against, so the argument is too vague to
be valid.

Please don't do that.  From now on, always state each position that
you try to refute.

>From 69f4f7ebb50c0d4fefccce3ecc4e5b893becd8d8 Mon Sep 17 00:00:00 2001
From: Nickolai Dobrynin <ndobrynin@gmail.com>
Date: Wed, 18 Nov 2026 01:19:38 +0100
Subject: [PATCH] Non-ASCII search queries in nnimap, via RFC 9755

* etc/NEWS: Announcement.  (Bug#81684)
---
 etc/NEWS | 13 +++++++++++++
 1 file changed, 13 insertions(+)

diff --git a/etc/NEWS b/etc/NEWS
index 640e27281f4..bb89a2d9558 100644
--- a/etc/NEWS
+++ b/etc/NEWS
@@ -755,6 +755,12 @@ natively compiled.
 Lisp programs may let-bind this variable to specify conditional actions
 for nested 'display-buffer' calls.
 
++++
+** New variable 'nnimap-native-utf8'.
+If non-'nil', enables native UTF-8 support in nnimap via RFC 9755
+(Bug#81684).  The variable is set per server and has no effect if
+the remote IMAP server lacks the "UTF8=ACCEPT" extension.
+
 +++
 ** New button to diff failed erts-file test output in ERT.
 When a test fails, the erts-file tests buffer displayed by
@@ -788,6 +794,13 @@ These functions convert between numbers and their Roman numeral forms.
 They were previously part of 'rst-mode' (as 'rst-arabic-to-roman' and
 'rst-roman-to-arabic'), but are now available as autoloaded functions.
 
+** Gnus
+*** Support for non-ASCII IMAP search queries
+Historically, making non-ASCII search queries relied on vendor-specific
+extensions.  The partial implementation of RFC 9755 (Bug#81684) adds
+unified support for arbitrary UTF-8 characters in search queries.  The
+"UTF8=ACCEPT" extension is necessary for this to work.
+

 filename=0001-Non-ASCII-search-queries-in-nnimap-via-RFC-9755.patch

>From fef8950097983b130d2585e4b787304887578209 Mon Sep 17 00:00:00 2001
From: Nickolai Dobrynin <ndobrynin@gmail.com>
Date: Wed, 18 Nov 2026 15:28:06 +0100
Subject: [PATCH] Non-ASCII search queries in nnimap, via RFC 9755

* etc/NEWS: Announcement.  (Bug#81684)
---
 etc/NEWS | 16 ++++++++++++++++
 1 file changed, 16 insertions(+)

diff --git a/etc/NEWS b/etc/NEWS
index 640e27281f4..3e4dc0d9415 100644
--- a/etc/NEWS
+++ b/etc/NEWS
@@ -589,6 +589,22 @@ weight in the United Kingdom and Ireland.
 ---
 *** A nil value for 'speedbar-file-unshown-regexp' means "show all".
 
+** Gnus
+
+---
+*** Support for non-ASCII IMAP search queries
+Historically, support for non-ASCII search queries relied on
+vendor-specific extensions.  The partial implementation of RFC 9755
+(Bug#81684) adds unified support for arbitrary UTF-8 characters in
+search queries.  The "UTF8=ACCEPT" extension is necessary for this
+to work.
+
+---
+*** New variable 'nnimap-native-utf8'.
+If non-'nil', enables native UTF-8 support in nnimap via RFC 9755
+(Bug#81684).  The variable is set per server and has no effect if
+the remote IMAP server lacks "UTF8=ACCEPT" extension.
+
 
 * New Modes and Packages in Emacs 32.1
 
-- 
2.55.0

Jean Louis <bugs@gnu.support> writes:

> Hello Philip,
>
> Thank you for taking the time to review the package and for your
> thoughtful feedback. I appreciate your consideration.
>
> I=E2=80=99m curious to learn more about the standards or criteria you use=
 when
> evaluating whether a package is suitable for ELPA. Could you perhaps
> share some insights on what you consider to be a good fit for the ELPA
> repository? This would help me better understand the rationale behind
> your initial impression.
>
> Author is doing calculations for TV stands. And you say it is not
> related to Emacs. So what is the standard for packages? They must
> relate to editor?
>
> I have here packages for mathematics, specific density, excavator
> production, construction and mining, and manufacturing, so is there
> standard that such subjects would be rejected as they do not improve
> the editor itself but packages give external utility?

I took a look at the package and then at the OP's github repo. Here are
some observations:

* The package implements a few trigonometric simple formulas for a very
  specific application, with some magic numbers thrown there.

* The package was LLM-generated, as its README says.

* The OP's github site contains multiple implementations of this package
  on various programming languages, all LLM generated.

* Apparently the OP is targeting languages with official or widely
  recognized repositories (the equivalent of our ELPAs.) Looks like each
  implementation meets the requirements (on terms of structure and
  metainfo) to be submitted to its respective repository.

* There are no implementations for popular languages that lack that type
  of standardized repository system, such as C and C++.

* The submitter's identity is a business. They offer a free online tool
  to do this type of calculations, which also acts as an entry to the
  sevices this business sells. The READMEs and other files of each
  package mentions the name of the business and contain links to the web
  site of the business or to the online tool or to both.

This looks to me as a SEO operation.

As this can be 100% automated, I'm afraid this type of submissions will
be a new kind of spam from now on for the ELPA maintainers.

On a more general note, it is a good thing to reject packages which are
low-effort *and* for a niche application, IMHO.

On Wed, Nov 18, 2026 at 04:42:07PM +0100, Nickolai Dobrynin wrote:
> Eli Zaretskii <eliz@gnu.org> writes:
>=20
> >> From: Nickolai Dobrynin <ndobrynin@gmail.com>
> >> Date: Wed, 18 Nov 2026 15:44:54 +0100
> >>=20
> >> Robert Pluim <rpluim@gmail.com> writes:
> >>=20
> >> > '+++' means you updated the manuals, but I can't see it there. Did y=
ou
> >> > mean '---'?
> >>=20
> >> I tried to mimic what other entries in that file did. Your explanation
> >> shows that I was mistaken.
> >
> > The explanation what "+++" and "---" mean is at the beginning of NEWS.
>=20
> Thanks. I can see them now. But the explanation does not say if the
> '+++' or '---' mark should go before or after the entry.

The '+++' typically marks the "new" file name, the "---" the "old",
corresponding to the line prefixes further down -- space meaning
no change (those are so-called "context lines", to help ensuring
that one is looking at the right thing) "-" means "delete this line"
(or "old"), "+" meaning "add". Then there are those "@@...@" to
denotate where in the file the action is. See, for example

  https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diff#Unified_format

The whole thing is called "unified diff format", and you get that
with

  diff -u <oldfile> <newfile>

(or just with "git diff").

Cheers
--=20
t

> The '+++' typically marks the "new" file name, the "---" the "old",
> corresponding to the line prefixes further down -- space meaning
> no change (those are so-called "context lines", to help ensuring
> that one is looking at the right thing) "-" means "delete this line"
> (or "old"), "+" meaning "add". Then there are those "@@...@" to
> denotate where in the file the action is. See, for example
> 
>   https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diff#Unified_format
> 
> The whole thing is called "unified diff format", and you get that
> with
> 
>   diff -u <oldfile> <newfile>
> 
> (or just with "git diff").

Thanks, but I think you answered the wrong question.  This was about
the markings in NEWS, not about unified diffs...

>From 3d69b3ee0d3c46e741b2d0de711e74839b8bb5d6 Mon Sep 17 00:00:00 2001
From: Nickolai Dobrynin <ndobrynin@gmail.com>
Date: Wed, 18 Nov 2026 18:24:00 +0100
Subject: [PATCH] Non-ASCII search queries in nnimap, via RFC 9755

* etc/NEWS: Announcement.  (Bug#81684)
---
 etc/NEWS | 16 ++++++++++++++++
 1 file changed, 16 insertions(+)

diff --git a/etc/NEWS b/etc/NEWS
index 640e27281f4..fcd20bd19ae 100644
--- a/etc/NEWS
+++ b/etc/NEWS
@@ -589,6 +589,22 @@ weight in the United Kingdom and Ireland.
 ---
 *** A nil value for 'speedbar-file-unshown-regexp' means "show all".
 
+** Gnus
+
+---
+*** Support for non-ASCII IMAP search queries.
+Historically, support for non-ASCII search queries relied on
+vendor-specific extensions.  The partial implementation of RFC 9755
+(Bug#81684) adds unified support for arbitrary UTF-8 characters in
+search queries.  The "UTF8=ACCEPT" extension is necessary for this
+to work.
+
+---
+*** New variable 'nnimap-native-utf8'.
+If non-'nil', enables native UTF-8 support in nnimap via RFC 9755
+(Bug#81684).  The variable is set per server and has no effect if
+the remote IMAP server lacks "UTF8=ACCEPT" extension.
+
 
 * New Modes and Packages in Emacs 32.1
 
--

> (Someone mentioned a program called Nuspell, but I don't know

% apt show nuspell
Package: nuspell
Version: 5.1.6-1+b1
Priority: optional
Section: text
Source: nuspell (5.1.6-1)
Maintainer: Thorsten Alteholz <debian@alteholz.de>
Installed-Size: 78.8 kB
Depends: libc6 (>= 2.34), libgcc-s1 (>= 3.0), libicu76 (>= 76.1-1~), libnuspell5 (>= 5.1.6), libstdc++6 (>= 13.1)
Homepage: http://nuspell.github.io/
Download-Size: 29.1 kB
APT-Sources: http://deb.debian.org/debian trixie/main amd64 Packages
Description: spell checker (program)
 Nuspell is a free and open source spell checker that is written in modern C++.
 It is designed for languages with rich morphology and complex word compounding.
 .
 Main features are:
  - Full unicode support backed by ICU
  - Backward compatibility with Hunspell dictionary file format
  - Twofold affix stripping (for agglutinative languages, like Azeri,
    Basque, Estonian, Finnish, Hungarian, Turkish, etc.)
  - Support complex compounds (for example, Hungarian, German and Dutch)
  - Support language specific features (for example, special casing of
    Azeri and Turkish dotted i, or German sharp s)
  - Handle conditional affixes, circumfixes, fogemorphemes, forbidden
    words, pseudoroots and homonyms.
 .
 This package contains the command-line program.

> If it is clearly tempting to use an LLM to port changes in Hunspell
> into vibe-spell, we cannot sensibly treat vibe-spell as independent
> source code.  We would betray our goal if we installed code whose
> maintenance depends on a nonfree program or SaaSS server.

I have reviewed the code and Augusto has applied my changes and others,
both by hand without the assistance of any LLMs.  For me, this
constitutes a proof that maintenance of the program does not rely on
LLMs.

> That would also add to the general pressure to yield to LLMs.  We will
> certainly face such general pressure, as people who don't feel concern
> about this issue try to insist we become dependent on LLMs.  We will
> face a struggle to refuse.  It would be foolish to choose to make that
> struggle harder.

I do not understand how this makes the struggle harder or easier?

> I am convinced that one requirement for including LLM-generated
> material in GNU Programs must be that the LLM-generated material be
> completely divorced from the LLM that generated it.  In other words,
> we must insist there be no reason to anticipate pressure to use LLMs
> to update it.  It must be source code, pure and simple, to be
> maintained like the rest of Emacs.

Just as a reminder, we are talking about a package to be added to NonGNU
ELPA, so this is not a GNU program, just by name.  And again, there is
no inherent reason why anyone would have to use an LLM to maintain
vibe-spell.

> In particular, LLM output should not be a machine translation of a
> source for which we expect further development.

* AND where we expect that it would be imperative to port changes from
the original in the translation AND where this job couldn't feasibly be
done by hand.

>
> 1. It could bring in copyright infringement and we might have to

Can you elaborate this point?  What infringements are you talking about?

> 2. It could create a situation where we face temptation, even pressure,
> to continue development of that program with LLMs, thus becoming
> a permanent dependence on LLMs.

Where is the boundary?  There are plenty of people that face the
temptation with any program, but we don't claim that the act of
maintaining software itself could create a permanent dependence.  What
if you use it to generate select boilerplate code?

>   > For me the most reasonable objection would be the 3k lines of code
>   > (~140K).  Yet I argue it cannot be the size of the package that

> You are trying to argue by reductio ad absurdam, but you haven't stated

> be valid.
>
> Please don't do that.  From now on, always state each position that
> you try to refute.

The claim here is that a common objection, one I have made myself in the
past, is that LLM generated code has a tendency to be overly verbose,
inlining functionality and lacking abstractions that would be intuitive
for humans.

Hi
I was playing around with the new speedbar window-mode in emacs 31 and had
some questions about further development.

1. Right now it leaves the window in fundamental mode rather than
speedbar-mode so many of the regular key mappings don't function.

2. There is no standard help for it when you press h unlike the convention
for most dedicated windows - even when speedbar-mode is on.

3. If you do a describe-mode several of the key bindings are lambdas that
don't display anything descriptive other than the bytecode and there are no
docstring help texts supplied.

(The theme here is the order in which i was investigating the UI)

There are further behaviors that are less basic that I think could be
improved. For example, the keymap shouldn't offer an option to kill the
frame when it's not in frame mode, hover text should work regardless of
whether the window is active etc.

For experimentation purposes, I ended up writing about 200 lines of code to
do enough wiring so it behaved more conventionally like other sidebars in
my own config.

The point of all this is I'm curious if I misunderstood how it's supposed
to work or if this is still in development,  and improvements are on tap
for version 32. Or is this an area where contributions would be helpful
Thanks
Ben

rejection or acceptance. But if it is -- please point to reference by 
GNU standard.

And it is not spam.

You say low effort, but please point out to exact GNU standard saying

effort.

Jean Louis <bugs@gnu.support> writes:

> Hello Philip,
>
> Thank you for taking the time to review the package and for your
> thoughtful feedback. I appreciate your consideration.
>
> I=E2=80=99m curious to learn more about the standards or criteria you use=
 when
> evaluating whether a package is suitable for ELPA. Could you perhaps
> share some insights on what you consider to be a good fit for the ELPA
> repository? This would help me better understand the rationale behind
> your initial impression.

First of all, I am not the only person who can add packages to ELPA, so
this is just my rationale.

Further than that, I would refer to the following two soft criteria from
https://elpa.gnu.org/contributing.html:

  Is a new package the right approach?

      If you are extending the functionality of an existing package, have
      you contacted the maintainer of said package to hear if they think
      your contribution would be worth upstreaming? Perhaps adding the
      feature directly to Emacs can simplify the implementation?

  Does the package constitute a significant contribution?

      If your package only defines a single, small function of a few
      lines, it might not be worth the effort to package. Keep in mind
      that every package constitutes a security risk if the maintainer's
      access to the repository gets compromised.

> Author is doing calculations for TV stands. And you say it is not
> related to Emacs. So what is the standard for packages? They must
> relate to editor?

I don't know if we can give a formal definition for the concern here,
namely is it an interesting contribution.  For me, the question is what
does this functionality have from being an Emacs package as opposed to
just a general, standalone executable that you can also just invoke from
Emacs -- M-x or M-! aren't that radically different, especially if the
package just prints the result using `message'.

> I have here packages for mathematics, specific density, excavator
> production, construction and mining, and manufacturing, so is there
> standard that such subjects would be rejected as they do not improve
> the editor itself but packages give external utility?

I would pose you the same question, why do you think it is interesting
as a package for a general audience, or do you think that it is the sort
of deal where you could publish the Lisp files on your own and tell
people, if you want to use them you can just drop them in your User Lisp
directory and that's it.  Especially considering the increasing risk of
supply chain issues, I think that the notion of having simple,
reviewable, hackable scripts that you can just adopt without having to
worry about upgrading is worth thinking about.

> Thank you again for your time and guidance.
>
> For the reference:
>

>> Just FTR that is not a criticism of the idea or the code, I am for now
>> trying to better understand the motivation behind the motivation of
>> having this as a package.

Philip Kaludercic <philipk@posteo.net> writes:

> Richard Stallman <rms@gnu.org> writes:
>> 1. It could bring in copyright infringement and we might have to
>> remove that file.
>
> Can you elaborate this point?  What infringements are you talking about?

I can provide one answer about risks: the Munich Court decided[1][2]
that for song lyrics, even if the use of some material as training data
is legal, it is still a copyrigt infringement if material generated by
an LLM reproduces a (potentially modified) version of parts of the
training data.

With the decision that the party responsible for that generation had to
pay a penalty and that it is not legal to exploit the generated
material (e.g. for money).

The responsible party as by the Munich decision was either the one
providing the model, or the one using it, or both to some degree,
depending on the complexity of the prompts. The more complex the
prompts, the more responsibility shifts to the user.

It is not clear, how courts will decide in the case of software. If they
follow the Munich decision, then any substantial part of code that=E2=80=99=
s too
similar to code in the training data violates the copyright of that part
of the training data (if no permission to reuse that material is given).

In a recent telecon by FSFE and nlnet[3], an FSFE lawyer said that the
legal situation is currently very much in flux, so no one knows what
the legal situation will be in a few years.

[1] the court decision (in German):
    https://www.gesetze-bayern.de/Content/Document/Y-300-Z-GRURRS-B-2025-N-=
30204
[2] article about the decision:
    https://www.twobirds.com/en/insights/2025/landmark-ruling-of-the-munich=
-regional-court-(gema-v-openai)-on-copyright-and-ai-training
[3] telecon held by nlnet in cooperasiot with FSFE (with recording and slid=
es):
    https://nlnet.nl/events/20261029/index.html

Best wishes,
Arne

I installed LuLu and then searched the device log via the Console app. =

pkg-config or perhaps to check versions. Not quite sure.=20

off` in a shell.

I=E2=80=99m not sure if that is a valid check. One can also execute

export HOMEBREW_NO_ANALYTICS=3D1

Before running ./configure to keep brew from emitting analytics.=20

[[[ To any NSA and FBI agents reading my email: please consider    ]]]
[[[ whether defending the US Constitution against all enemies,     ]]]
[[[ foreign or domestic, requires you to follow Snowden's example. ]]]

  > In my view, one of the "soft" targets of free software now in
  > peril is "software as a conversation between humans", which I
  > think lies at the core of software's Freedom 1 (study) and
  > Freedom 3 (improve). I sure want to know if I'm talking to
  > a human or a machine (especially if the latter is controlled
  > by a huge company).

I see your point.  It is a different point from the concern about
the bobsled of surrender to digital agents.

What is not clear to me is how we could prevent that.  Without strict
secrecy, these huge companies will be able to read our public mailing
lists.  And humans can also be agents of a huge company, passing along
what they see.  But strict secrecy would damage our community even
worse.

[[[ To any NSA and FBI agents reading my email: please consider    ]]]
[[[ whether defending the US Constitution against all enemies,     ]]]
[[[ foreign or domestic, requires you to follow Snowden's example. ]]]

  > One of the valid issues is that spelling tools based on ispell as 
  > suboptimal and alternatives like jinx - of which I'm a happy user- are 
  > sometimes difficult to spin up, because they depend on a C module that 
  > may be non-trivial to generate on some systems.

Could you please state which systems those are?  I have a hunch that
they are non-GNU systems, and another hunch that they are nonfree.
Are my hunches correct?

I explained recently that we encourage people to port GNU software to
non-GNU systems if they want to.  But this issue raises a different
issue: how much importance should the GNU Project give to supporting
non-GNU systems, and non-free systems?

Specifically, should we go to extra trouble to make it easier to support
those systems?  Should we subject ourselves to burdens in our own work
(such as, maintaining with LLM-generated code) for the sake of that support?
For instance, features that affect whether jinx can be used on them?

You've proposed reimplementing jinx with a new interace to make it
less work to support those systems.  So far, it sounds ok to me, if
someone volunteers to do that work.  It would only affect jinx, which
is rather localized, so it wouldn't be a major design change or
a major distraction.

A new general "foreign function interface" could be a lot more work,
and has the major drawback that Eli just pointed out.

On 2026-11-19 05:30, Richard Stallman wrote:
> [[[ To any NSA and FBI agents reading my email: please consider    ]]]
> [[[ whether defending the US Constitution against all enemies,     ]]]
> [[[ foreign or domestic, requires you to follow Snowden's example. ]]]
> 
> This seems like a big concern.
> 
>   > I don't know of a project which has avoided these problems without
>   > a ban. I have read about projects like the game engine Bevy where 
> they
>   > had a ban but then lifted it, and it went very badly:
> 
>   > https://blog.fallible.net/it-breaks-a-village/
> 
>   > Projects like this where they try to find a middle ground and 
> require
>   > that LLM usage must be "responsible" or "human guided only" don't
>   > usually end up successful in those criteria over time due to the 
> "vibe
>   > bobsled" problem I mentioned earlier.
> 
> I wonder if a free LLM, usable locally, could make it possible to
> adapt the LLM such that it won't do this.

Yes, a free LLM that runs locally could absolutely be adapted so it does 
not do this, and that is exactly why the problem should be solved at the 
model level instead of just banning contributions. The failures 
mentioned happened with proprietary, hosted models, where the community 
could not inspect, change, or constrain the tool at all. A genuinely 
free local model is different: you can fine-tune it, audit it, configure 
it, and under collective control in a way no commercial service ever is. 
The real catch is that today's models like Qwen are not truly free 
because their training data isn't, and that tells us what the 
free-software movement should actually do: push to build the free LLM, 
not treat LLMs as inherently corrosive. That is the same move GNU made 
with proprietary tools — build the free replacement instead of banning 
the use.

-- 
Jean Louis

Philip Kaludercic <philipk@posteo.net> writes:

>>> * Apparently the OP is targeting languages with official or widely
>>>   recognized repositories (the equivalent of our ELPAs.) Looks like
>>> each
>>>   implementation meets the requirements (on terms of structure and
>>>   metainfo) to be submitted to its respective repository.
>>
>> You are here implying bad faith or bad intentions with "targeting". It
>> is better to assume good faith.
>
> In general perhaps yes, but this does sound suspicious in a way that I
> don't think we should ignore.  The "bad intentions" being assumed here
> is that they want to publish these packages as a means of distributing
> malware in the long term.

I don't think so. As you know, the dirty part of SEO (Search Engine
Optimization) is to place links to your site together with the key words
related to it on as many other sites as possible. But not all places are
equal: for sure elpa.(non)gnu.org adds more points to the page rank than
some abandoned forum full of spam (which actually can subtract points!)
Same can be said about the package repositories of those other
programming languages that the OP targets.

On this specific case, I'm pretty sure that the intention is to use elpa
for boosting their web site on the search engines.

Thanks to LLMs, doing this now is pretty trivial. The only obstacule for
them is the repositories' gatekeepers (thanks!) so they have to submit
something minimally credible, but still related to their bussines for
the relevant words being present on the same context as the links.

Your concerns about malware are justified, but that's a diferent kind of
operation. For starters, the submitted package that acts as a trojan
horse needs to be as attractive as possible for the target population.
Which now also can be achieved at a tiny fraction of the cost that used
to have.

This is related to the other discussion about accepting LLM-generated
packages. It is very easy to produce a working, useful package that is
very hard to review, because of a combination of size, complexity and
obfuscation.

Richard Stallman <rms@gnu.org> writes:

[...]

> I am convinced that one requirement for including LLM-generated 
> material in GNU Programs must be that the LLM-generated material 
> be completely divorced from the LLM that generated it.  In other 
> words, we must insist there be no reason to anticipate pressure 
> to use LLMs to update it.

I've thought for some time this is a key point, but unfortunately 
subjective. Emacs maintainers, being proficient in elisp, would 
probably not feel pressure to use an LLM, assuming the initial use 
produced decent code (as Philip seems to be saying is the case 
with this package).

But someone less proficient who wishes to use a package like 
vibe-spell as an opportunity to contribute, and to enter the 
community, on hearing that it was originally authored by an LLM 
would, I believe, be inclined to ease their own entry to the 
community by also using an LLM.

I believe this constitutes "pressure", and is a danger to the 
wider (potential) community, even though it is probably not a 
feeling experienced by maintainers in the same position.

Thanks and regards,

       - Joel

Jean Louis <bugs@gnu.support> writes:

> Hello Philip,
>
> I have asked twice for standard to justify rejection criteria such as
> SEO, low-effort, business identity and instead of answering what is
> the standard you just reframe position, deflect (that you do not need
> to restrict to GNU standard), and turn the question back on me.
>
> So the standard is your discretionary judgment.
>
> I don't find it welcoming.

First of all, for the concrete package, the submitter themselves has
retracted their proposal, so that should close the case.

Second of all, I didn't directly reject the package, but just asked the
submitter to explain why they thought that the package was a good
addition to the archive.

Everyone who helps maintain and curate ELPA has different standards by
necessity, and to some degree they are a matter of taste.  I don't know
what Stefan would have said about the package, for instance, and if we
were to be OK with it, I wouldn't have made that into a problem.

I think that Oscar makes a valid point of that this is a package that
seems to have such a limited and specific utility that it doesn't appear
to be interesting _as_ a package, but just exists to improve the SEO
rating of some other website -- and we have no responsibility to help
with that.

But technically, my main concern was that this just felt too small to be
a package.  I have explained my position on this in a previous message
in this thread.  And yes, this is a judgment call, not some formal rule.

Joel Reicher <joel.reicher@gmail.com> writes:

> Richard Stallman <rms@gnu.org> writes:
>
> [...]
>
>> I am convinced that one requirement for including LLM-generated
>> material in GNU Programs must be that the LLM-generated material be
>> completely divorced from the LLM that generated it.  In other words,
>> we must insist there be no reason to anticipate pressure to use LLMs
>> to update it.
>
> I've thought for some time this is a key point, but unfortunately
> subjective. Emacs maintainers, being proficient in elisp, would
> probably not feel pressure to use an LLM, assuming the initial use
> produced decent code (as Philip seems to be saying is the case with
> this package).
>
> But someone less proficient who wishes to use a package like
> vibe-spell as an opportunity to contribute, and to enter the
> community, on hearing that it was originally authored by an LLM would,
> I believe, be inclined to ease their own entry to the community by
> also using an LLM.

I would be interested to hear your opinion of the source code and
whether or not you find it to be understandable, setting aside the fine
technicalities of spell checking (which I understand aren't easy to do).

Initially I wanted to suggest some low hanging feature that you could
hack on as an exercise to see how easy or difficult it is for you, and
perhaps Augusto has an idea, but it also occured to me that by using
LLMs in the first draft of the package, it might very well me that this
fact just takes care of most "low hanging" features -- and I think it is
important that we don't confuse the relative exhaustiveness of the code
generation with the inability to maintain the code.

> I believe this constitutes "pressure", and is a danger to the wider
> (potential) community, even though it is probably not a feeling
> experienced by maintainers in the same position.

I am not that convinced that this is "pressure" in the strong sense that
would be necessary to substantiate the argument.  If you have reasons or
principles against using LLMs for code generation (as I do), then this
pressure will not make you change your mind.  And I don't see why
inexperience of uncertainty wouldn't generally create the same sense of
"pressure" to use LLMs for other packages as well.  I think your point
is that "if LLMs have been used it the past, then it doesn't matter if I
use them in the future", right?

Perhaps a far out idea, but what would you say if Augusto added a "no
(further) LLM contributions" clause to the package?

> Thanks and regards,
>
>       - Joel

invoking speedbar-window-mode interactively (as opposed to customizing

Hi Richard,

Answers inline...

On 19/11/26 3:29, Richard Stallman wrote:
> [[[ To any NSA and FBI agents reading my email: please consider    ]]]
> [[[ whether defending the US Constitution against all enemies,     ]]]
> [[[ foreign or domestic, requires you to follow Snowden's example. ]]]
> 
>    > One of the valid issues is that spelling tools based on ispell as
>    > suboptimal and alternatives like jinx - of which I'm a happy user- are
>    > sometimes difficult to spin up, because they depend on a C module that
>    > may be non-trivial to generate on some systems.
> 
> Could you please state which systems those are?  I have a hunch that
> they are non-GNU systems, and another hunch that they are nonfree.
> Are my hunches correct?

To a certain extent, they are (mea culpa).  But this is not my main 
motivation.
> You've proposed reimplementing jinx with a new interace to make it
> less work to support those systems.  So far, it sounds ok to me, if
> someone volunteers to do that work.  It would only affect jinx, which
> is rather localized, so it wouldn't be a major design change or
> a major distraction.

Let's step back one step: if aspell/ispell was fast enough, there 
wouldn't be any need to start talking about other spellchecking 
strategies. But, unfortunately, they aren't.

This is, how I understand it, why some people look into other 
strategies, jinx being one of them. JINX implies compiling a module, 
which requires a gcc infrastructure to be installed.

On older, more constrained systems I'm keeping alive to use when on the 
move (I use Linux or FreeBSD on those), this means less space for my data.

So, as a challenge to myself, I've been looking at something based on a 
JSONRPC using libenchant. And when the whole LLM thing came up, I 
suggested this alternative path.
> A new general "foreign function interface" could be a lot more work,
> and has the major drawback that Eli just pointed out.
And I wholeheartedly agree with him.

> Date: Thu, 19 Nov 2026 08:11:10 +0300
> From: Jean Louis <bugs@gnu.support>

>  jporterbugs@gmail.com, emacs-devel@gnu.org
> 
> > I wonder if a free LLM, usable locally, could make it possible to
> > adapt the LLM such that it won't do this.
> 
> Yes, a free LLM that runs locally could absolutely be adapted so it does 
> not do this, and that is exactly why the problem should be solved at the 
> model level instead of just banning contributions.

Only if LLM is supposed to be used as part of future development or
maintenance of some package or part of Emacs.  If an LLM was used for
a change or a package, but is not supposed to be used thereafter to
maintain the change/package, which tools the author used for producing
the code is none of our concern.  Exactly like we don't reject code
produced by a proprietary editor or compiled and tested using
proprietary compiler, as long as after we accept the code, we use free
tools for its further development and maintenance.

> The real catch is that today's models like Qwen are not truly free 
> because their training data isn't, and that tells us what the 
> free-software movement should actually do: push to build the free LLM, 
> not treat LLMs as inherently corrosive. That is the same move GNU made 
> with proprietary tools — build the free replacement instead of banning 
> the use.

Training data will unlikely to ever become completely free, because
any decent model needs extremely large quantities of training data,
and there's no practical way of having that if being free is a
constraint.  Most publicly accessible data on the Internet is not
free, in the legal sense pertinent to this discussion.  So IMO the
industry and the GNU project will have to find a way of living with
this caveat, if the decision is that LLM-generated code is acceptable
by GNU.

who curate ELPA) do a wonderful job; if you want to change any of its
aspects, you need to volunteer to be part of the team, accept some of
their responsibilities, and do some of the job they do.  Until then,
you are not entitled to demand Philip to give you detailed report
about his criteria and decisions.  It's an accepted rule in volunteer
projects that whoever does a job is entitled to decide on its aspects
where those need a judgment call.

I'm not sure whether this is a bug, so I wanted to ask. In places where
an overlay is displayed, if whitespace-mode is enabled, the
whitespace-mode face gets overridden by the overlay's face. Please see
the image for details.

To reproduce the effect in the image, please enable eglot and 
(setq flymake-show-diagnostics-at-end-of-line 'fancy).



Or you can run the following code.

test code
```emacs-lisp
(let ((ov (make-overlay (point-max) (point-max))))
  (overlay-put ov 'after-string
               (propertize "test test" 'face '(:foreground "red"))))
```

1. emacs -Q
2. C-x C-e
3. M-x whitespace-mode RET

> Richard Stallman <rms@gnu.org> writes:
> 
> [...]
> 
> > I am convinced that one requirement for including LLM-generated 
> > material in GNU Programs must be that the LLM-generated material 
> > be completely divorced from the LLM that generated it.  In other 
> > words, we must insist there be no reason to anticipate pressure 
> > to use LLMs to update it.
> 
> I've thought for some time this is a key point, but unfortunately 
> subjective. Emacs maintainers, being proficient in elisp, would 
> probably not feel pressure to use an LLM, assuming the initial use 
> produced decent code (as Philip seems to be saying is the case 
> with this package).
> 
> But someone less proficient who wishes to use a package like 
> vibe-spell as an opportunity to contribute, and to enter the 
> community, on hearing that it was originally authored by an LLM 
> would, I believe, be inclined to ease their own entry to the 
> community by also using an LLM.

I think you've misunderstood what Richard wanted to convey.  Note that
he explicitly said "divorced from the LLM that generated it".  My
interpretation of this is that we should not be _forced_ to use the
_same_ LLM to continue developing such code.

However, it is quite possible that someone other than the person who
submitted the code will, at some future date, submit further changes
and improvements for that code, and that other person could use LLM to
produce or assist in production of these further changes.  If
LLM-generated code is acceptable at all, there's no practical way to
ensure this will not happen, because, once admitted into Emacs, the
original LLM-generated code is not different from any other code in
Emacs.  And it is unreasonable to expect the Emacs project to track,
for each line of Emacs sources, whether they were at some point in the
past modified by LLM-generated changes, and then disallow any further
LLM-generated changes for those lines.

IOW, what I think Richard says is that we should not accept the
situation where some code in Emacs _must_ be developed or maintained
using LLMs, but there's no objection to _allow_ such LLM-generated
changes if that's one of the alternatives, alongside changes produced
entirely by humans.

> I believe this constitutes "pressure", and is a danger to the 
> wider (potential) community, even though it is probably not a 
> feeling experienced by maintainers in the same position.

I don't see how a possibility (but not necessity) of using LLMs could
be considered "pressure".  Such a conclusion is against my intuitive
understanding of what constitutes "pressure".  For any aspect like
this to constitute "pressure", the alternatives must be either
forbidden or at least punitive or much less attractive to _everyone_.
Like, for example, our clear preference to extend Emacs in Lisp rather
than in C.  That some people might decide, given their personal
situations and preferences, to use this or that alternative, does not
come close to "pressure" in my book.

Eli Zaretskii <eliz@gnu.org> writes:

> IOW, what I think Richard says is that we should not accept the
> situation where some code in Emacs _must_ be developed or maintained
> using LLMs, but there's no objection to _allow_ such LLM-generated
> changes if that's one of the alternatives, alongside changes produced
> entirely by humans.

What I thought I understood is that there need not only be one
alternative to contribute without an LLM, but that this alternative
should be the preferred one.

If that=E2=80=99s not the case, there=E2=80=99s a problem, because it incen=
tivizes
people into using proprietary software and/or SaaSS.

>> I believe this constitutes "pressure", and is a danger to the=20
>> wider (potential) community, even though it is probably not a=20
>> feeling experienced by maintainers in the same position.
>
> I don't see how a possibility (but not necessity) of using LLMs could
> be considered "pressure".  Such a conclusion is against my intuitive
> understanding of what constitutes "pressure".  For any aspect like
> this to constitute "pressure", the alternatives must be either
> forbidden or at least punitive or much less attractive to _everyone_.

A possibility could be that most of the code gets rewritten again and
again (while having only little progress in features), such that humans
cannot incrementally get an understanding of the code. That way they
have no mental model they can build upon and cannot work with
the code efficiently.

This is from the experience that I received a huge commit for review
this summer with the note by the contributor that they didn=E2=80=99t split=
 it
into individual, clean commits, because every added step of the LLM
caused unrelated changes, so in the end they squashed it all.

Best wishes,
Arne

ohne es zu merken.

I was able to build and run it successfully on Windows, so I=E2=80=99ll add=
 the
instructions here:

1. Use the MSYS2 toolchain.
2. Run pacman -S mingw-w64-ucrt-x86_64-pkgconf mingw-w64-ucrt-x86_64-libmup=
df.
3. In Emacs, run M-x emureader-build RET.

Here=E2=80=99s a summary of the issues I ran into:

1. If .dll is not included in load-suffixes, Emacs won=E2=80=99t find
emureader-dyn.dll.
2. The native Windows sort command takes precedence over MSYS2=E2=80=99s so=
rt.
The Windows version is located at /c/Windows/system32/sort.

Eli Zaretskii <eliz@gnu.org> writes:

[...]

(Going to respond to the elided part separately, at a later time)

>> I believe this constitutes "pressure", and is a danger to the 
>> wider (potential) community, even though it is probably not a 
>> feeling experienced by maintainers in the same position.
>
> I don't see how a possibility (but not necessity) of using LLMs 
> could be considered "pressure".  Such a conclusion is against my 
> intuitive understanding of what constitutes "pressure".

This is why I mentioned the subjectivity of it.

My own experience of this kind of "pressure" is in a slightly 
different area: use of Emacs's Info pages. I know from experience 
that not only are many (newish) Emacs users unaware of the Info 
pages; they resist using the Info pages once becoming aware. There 
are various factors to this, but perhaps the biggest is the 
availability of the documents on the web.

The web is a familiar form of access (viewing, and somewhat more 
significantly, searching) and although it's an unusual way to view 
the behaviour I would suggest the availability of the web 
constitutes "pressure" to use it INSTEAD of the Info pages.

I myself use the Info pages heavily - almost exclusively - and I 
do not feel this "pressure" at all. But I see it clearly in the 
behaviour of other users (and regularly try to change their minds 
about it).

I am quite convinced the availability of using an LLM to write 
elisp will do the same; users will feel "pressure" not to write 
elisp themselves. This is so clear to me that I don't even think 
it's a point that needs to be established; I regard it as fact.

Rather I think the main argument is whether increasing dependence 
on LLMs in the Emacs community, and a decrease in actual 
understanding of elisp, constitutes harm to the community.

> For any aspect like this to constitute "pressure", the 
> alternatives must be either forbidden or at least punitive or 
> much less attractive to _everyone_.

I think a weakening of the last possibility is both true and 
sufficient; the alternatives must be "much less attractive" to 
"enough people". The question here (IMO) is harm to the community 
at large; not harm to "everyone".

And this is where I think the contentious "outright ban" stance 
comes from: to prevent LLMs being "too attractive" for SOME 
people, they need to be disallowed (or somesuch) for 
everyone. That is (if you don't mind me putting it so crudely), 
the negation of a "some" is the "all" of a negation.

Thanks and regards,

       - Joel

Philip Kaludercic <philipk@posteo.net> writes:

> Joel Reicher <joel.reicher@gmail.com> writes:

[...]

>> But someone less proficient who wishes to use a package like 
>> vibe-spell as an opportunity to contribute, and to enter the 
>> community, on hearing that it was originally authored by an LLM 
>> would, I believe, be inclined to ease their own entry to the 
>> community by also using an LLM.
>
> I would be interested to hear your opinion of the source code 
> and whether or not you find it to be understandable, setting 
> aside the fine technicalities of spell checking (which I 
> understand aren't easy to do).

There are some relatively large boolean expressions that stand out 
to me as sufficiently difficult to understand that a human would 
have written them differently.

It doesn't mean they can't be understood; rather it adds to the 
fatigue of the code being harder to understand than is necessary 
(in my opinion).

[...]

>> I believe this constitutes "pressure", and is a danger to the 
>> wider (potential) community, even though it is probably not a 
>> feeling experienced by maintainers in the same position.
>
> I am not that convinced that this is "pressure" in the strong 
> sense that would be necessary to substantiate the argument.  If 
> you have reasons or principles against using LLMs for code 
> generation (as I do), then this pressure will not make you 
> change your mind.  And I don't see why inexperience of 
> uncertainty wouldn't generally create the same sense of 
> "pressure" to use LLMs for other packages as well.

In my experience it's a fairly consistent aspect of human nature 
that if a person is uncertain how to proceed in their own work, 
they will take their cue from their community.

I think inexperience and uncertainly does not create a sense of 
"pressure"; rather it makes a person vulnerable to influences they 
can't judge the merit of. So it's the presence and immediacy of 
that influence or example that matters, which is why something 
like this package might be more influential than exposure to code 
not authored by an LLM.

> I think your point is that "if LLMs have been used it the past, 
> then it doesn't matter if I use them in the future", right?

No, a bit stronger than that. "I'm struggling to do this, but it 
seemed when they used an LLM it was easier for them, so I think I 
should try that too."

> Perhaps a far out idea, but what would you say if Augusto added 
> a "no (further) LLM contributions" clause to the package?

I think that would address a lot of what I'm describing, for this 
package. Not sure it's practical as a general rule though.

Thanks and regards,

       - Joel

On 2026-11-18 at 21:30, <rms@gnu.org> wrote:

> I wonder if a free LLM, usable locally, could make it possible to
> adapt the LLM such that it won't do this.

There is no such thing as a =E2=80=9Cfree LLM=E2=80=9D. LLMs are made out o=
f:

(0) Program. The model as an executable might be gratis, i.e.
downloadable without charge. Nice.

(1) Code. The source code might be free. Nice!

(2) Expertise. Big Tech increasingly isolates their respective AI
research and does not share it publicly. Still, for the clever
hacker community, this might be the least of problems.

(3) Data. The amount of data needed to train an LLM to a usable
level of intelligence is not available to the public. There are
public datasets to download but they are too small. You could
scrape the web but nowadays many websites require proof of work,
cookies and Javascript, i.e. a full browser, which makes it
unscrapable without a data centers or botnets. Big Tech companies
like Meta and Google (which cooperates with Reddit) do their best
to prevent scraping of their walled gardens so that they can keep
their data to train their own *large* language models.

A model might be pre-trained and =E2=80=98open weight=E2=80=99, but if the
training and post-training data is missing, you cannot bootstrap
the weights yourself. You'll still dependent on the actor that has
trained the model with the data.

(4) Compute. To train a model on the data, you need enormous
amount of compute that is only possible with giant data centers.
You cannot do this as a loosely organized collective of hackers.
But you'll depend on data centers of Big Tech.

Note that the compute power you need for inference, i.e. to =E2=80=98run
the model locally=E2=80=99 is something different: Many models run on
computers that cost around 5000 USD (if you buy graphics cards
second hand) and are thus affordable for some well-earning, senior
software engineers in the Global North.


=E2=80=9CFree LLM=E2=80=9D is a hypothetical, utopian term. Questions like =
=E2=80=98if we
had a free, local LLM, would ...?=E2=80=99 thus don't make sense to me.

Mekeor Melire <mekeor@posteo.de> writes:

> On 2026-11-18 at 21:30, <rms@gnu.org> wrote:
>
>> I wonder if a free LLM, usable locally, could make it possible to
>> adapt the LLM such that it won't do this.
>
> (4) Compute. To train a model on the data, you need enormous
> amount of compute that is only possible with giant data centers.
> You cannot do this as a loosely organized collective of hackers.
> But you'll depend on data centers of Big Tech.

If someone could

1. collect and tag Free Software and Free Culture material for model
   training and then

2. adapt the training process to ensure that attribution is preserved
   (which parts of the training data informed the neurons that get
   activated by a given request), then

3. it could be possible to build something like a SETI@home to train a
   truly free LLM that does not only generate output but also provides
   attribution to its sources and ensures license compliance (if (A)GPL
   code is included in the training data that influenced the activated
   neurons, then the project must be licensed under (A)GPL and each part
   must be (A)GPL-compatible).

But until 1 and 2 are fulfilled, there=E2=80=99s no reason to take into acc=
ount
the theoretical viability of 3 when discussing project policy.

Hi Stefan,

Stefan Monnier <monnier@iro.umontreal.ca> writes:

>     [...]
> and Org seems to generate the following from it:
>     [...]

Sorry for the trouble. The cause is on my side: `#+BEGIN_HTML' has not
been an export block since Org 8.0. Current Org reads it as a special
block named "HTML", so its contents are parsed as Org text, which gives
the escaped tags and the bare image URLs turned into <img> that you saw.

> Github happily displays this Org's content as a table of screenshots
> (https://github.com/szymonwilczek/au-themes/blob/main/README.org), but
> my Org/HTML-fu is not strong enough to understand why.

GitHub renders Org with org-ruby, which still knows only the old syntax.
It treats `#+BEGIN_HTML' as raw HTML, but it would hide a
`#+BEGIN_EXPORT html' block, so the modern form would remove the gallery
from GitHub. The single-line `#+HTML:' keyword works in both, so I have
switched the README to it, and also gave the headings the internal links
point to a CUSTOM_ID. It is now in the repo.

> Can someone shed some light on this (so I can improve `elpa-admin.el` to
> fix the false positives above)?

The messages come from the regexp in `elpaa--doc-html-adjust-auxfiles',
which matched ` src="<img src="' inside the escaped text.

I've attached the patch that requires the attribute to be inside a real
tag (the FIXME next to that loop). With my old README it goes from 18
matches to none, and it still finds relative `src' attributes, including
in tags over several lines. It also stops the old regexp from rewriting
escaped text such as `&lt;img src="foo.png"' when a file of that name
exists. Hope this helps.

Thanks,
Szymon


--=-=-=
Content-Type: text/x-patch
Content-Disposition: inline;
 filename=0001-elpa-admin.el-Only-rewrite-src-attributes-found-insi.patch

>From daaa56afef6daa9312db330708cf160a33695f66 Mon Sep 17 00:00:00 2001
From: Szymon Wilczek <swilczek.lx@gmail.com>
Date: Thu, 19 Nov 2026 18:10:00 +0100
Subject: [PATCH] elpa-admin.el: Only rewrite `src' attributes found inside
 tags

* elpa-admin.el (elpaa--doc-html-adjust-auxfiles): Require the `src'
attribute to be inside a tag, and the file name not to contain `<' or
`>'.  This skips text that only looks like an attribute, such as
escaped HTML in a paragraph.
---
 elpa-admin.el | 3 +--

+++ b/elpa-admin.el
@@ -3105,7 +3105,7 @@ directory; one of archive, archive-devel."
   ;; (let* ((auxfiles (elpaa--spec-get pkg-spec :doc-files)))
   ;;  (when auxfiles
   (let* ((docdir (if (stringp docfile) (file-name-directory docfile)))
-         (regexp " \\(?:src\\)=\"\\([^#/.\"][^:\"#]+\\)\""))
+         (regexp "<[[:alpha:]][^<>]*[ \t\n]src=\"\\([^#/.\"<>][^:\"#<>]*\\)\""))
     (with-current-buffer (if (stringp html-file)
                              (find-file-noselect html-file)
                            html-file)
@@ -3115,7 +3115,6 @@ directory; one of archive, archive-devel."
         (elpaa--message "default-directory=%S" default-directory)
         (goto-char (point-min))
         (let ((case-fold-search t))
-          ;; FIXME: Skip false positives found outside of tags!
           (while (re-search-forward regexp nil t)
             (message "found match for: %S" (match-string 1))
             (let* ((file (match-string 1))

Eli Zaretskii <eliz@gnu.org> writes:

>> Eli Zaretskii <eliz@gnu.org> writes:

[...]

>>> I see no harm here, except to people who harm themselves.
>>>
>>> With all due respect, we are not a kindergarten.
>>
>> Yes, but there is still such a thing as a newcomer to Emacs, 
>> and  to the community.
>
> And they are very welcome, and receive our support and guidance. 
> But telling them not to harm themselves is not our job.

I think this might overstate the potential problem to an extent 
that misses the point.

If I see someone using bash and pressing the up arrow 20 times to 
get back to something they know is in their history and want to 
use, I will almost certainly let them know about the "history" 
command and the "!..." expansions.

I'm not sure it's accurate to say they have done themselves harm 
not seeking this out previously - it is more like a lost 
opportunity - and that is probably why I see an obligation for 
myself to point it out.

If it was indeed deliberate self-harm, I might agree with you and 
not feel such an obligation, but I'm not sure it is.

[...]

>>> The stance that "we know better what's good for you" is IMO a 
>>> disservice to our users.  I hope GNU will never go there.  If 
>>> it ever does, I'll be outta here, given some firsthand 
>>> experience I have with such regimes.
>>
>> I have a lot of sympathy for that, and I'm no fan of 
>> paternalism  (or worse), but I'm convinced there is such a 
>> thing as leadership  that doesn't fall afoul of the kinds of 
>> concerns you describe.
>
> Cannot agree more, but where's the evidence that we don't 
> provide exactly such kind of leadership?

You absolutely do provide leadership on matters you believe to be 
relevant to Emacs.

So I think this debate is about relevance. For example we can 
agree that various forms of deliberate "self-harm" by some users 
is not relevant. (That's a weird example but I hope it makes 
sense.)

But I think the lost opportunity to learn elisp by instead 
favouring LLM use is less clear. In my experience learning elisp 
is a large and invaluable part of the Emacs experience, and I say 
that as someone who avoided learning elisp for the first 5 years 
of my own use. The fact I now regard that as a great shame is a 
large part of why I'm now arguing against LLMs.

Thanks and regards,

       - Joel

>> Actually, no, this is still O(N=B2) on `master` as well, still (the rege=
xp
>> search causes O(N) calls to `re_match` and *that* one is reduced to
>> O(N)).
> Ah, thanks for the explanation, I had missed that. On Emacs 31 my
> timings grew linearly for the inputs I tried, but I can't rule out
> a worse case.

In normal circumstances it's linear, indeed.

> - as you said, nobody has hit a real false positive yet, so it only
>   fixes a problem that doesn't exist in practice so far.

Also, IIRC the code is fairly safe in that false positives are harmless
because we detect them "reliably" by checking for the presence of the
corresponding file, so they simply emit a warning message.

> If you think it's worth it now, or once a real case shows up, I'm
> happy to send it as a patch.  If not, no problem.

I think I'll keep the current simplistic search for now.
Maybe the only real fix we need is to make sure we don't let a false
positive hide a real positive (which we could do by going back to (1+
(match-beginning 0)) before the next iteration of the search).


=3D=3D=3D Stefan

wrote:

> If someone could
>
> 1. collect and tag Free Software and Free Culture material for model
>    training and then

I believe I understand your post, and I agree with it. There is a
further important "wrinkle" that, based on current technology, there
are quite strong reasons to believe that there is insufficient
material to, let's say "use as input for point one above" currently in
existence, and it's not close. This suggests either a big revision to
point one, or a necessary (and potentially difficult, on practical and
political spectra, as well as technical) point zero.

Probably, most people in this conversation understand this to some
degree, but _as I read the conversations_, it seems like some of
those messages are ignoring or skipping this point. Perhaps those
messages' authors mean to imply some sort of future development
that overcomes this hurdle. Sadly, there is not much effort on that
front at the moment, at least as far as I can tell. (Lots of people agree
that it would be good if "someone" could do this, but basically nobody
is seriously trying it themselves. "Why" is a different conversation.)

It seems (again, to me) highly likely that a more-or-less global change
in copyright policy is *more* likely, at least in the next decade or so. (I
would go farther and speculate that the most likely path involves another
AI Winter, but that's also a different conversation.)

I hope that helps get some assumptions out in the open.
~Chad

chad <yandros@gmail.com> writes:

> are quite strong reasons to believe that there is insufficient
> material to, let's say "use as input for point one above" currently in
> existence, and it's not close. This suggests either a big revision to
> point one, or a necessary (and potentially difficult, on practical and
> political spectra, as well as technical) point zero.

Or it needs more development on efficient training in point 2 (adapt
training to preserve attribution).

It may need quite a bit of research.

I list the training data as point 1, because having collected and
properly tagged (with author, copyright holder, and license) training
data is a requirement for any path towards a Free LLM.

If working LLM code generation should prove to be impossible with
legally reproducable training data, this training data could still be
useful as a base for a search index to locate existing free licensed
code or patches which can solve a problem at hand.

Best wishes,

Stefan Monnier <monnier@iro.umontreal.ca> writes:

> Actually, no, this is still O(N=C2=B2) on `master` as well, still (the re=
gexp
> search causes O(N) calls to `re_match` and *that* one is reduced to
> O(N)).

Ah, thanks for the explanation, I had missed that. On Emacs 31 my
timings grew linearly for the inputs I tried, but I can't rule out a
worse case.

I also found another problem with my regexp: on a tag longer than about
300 KB the [^<>]* part fails with "Stack overflow in regexp matcher".
So please drop that patch.

An alternative that avoids both problems is to stop matching attributes
with a regexp and walk the tags instead: find "<" followed by a letter,
then read the attributes one by one (name, optional =3D, then a "..." or
'...' or bare value) until ">". Each character is looked at once and
none of the regexps can backtrack over a long span, so it's linear and
doesn't overflow the stack. In my tests it:

- finds nothing in the HTML from my old README and nothing in the new
  one,
- still finds relative src values in tags spanning several lines, with
  single quotes or no quotes, and when another attribute's value
  contains ">",
- skips escaped text like &lt;img src=3D"foo.png", and src=3D inside another
  attribute's value,
- takes 0.01 s on a 1.6 MB data: URI and grows linearly elsewhere.

But of course, it has some limits:

- it's about maybe 20 lines of code instead of one regexp,
- it isn't a real HTML parser: it doesn't skip the contents of <script>,
  <style> or <!-- comments --> (but neither does the current code),
- as you said, nobody has hit a real false positive yet, so it only
  fixes a problem that doesn't exist in practice so far.

If you think it's worth it now, or once a real case shows up, I'm happy
to send it as a patch. If not, no problem.

Thanks,
Szymon

Hi

I would like to request that the function 
(completion--selected-candidate) is "promoted" to 
(completion-selected-candidate).

The use case:

I'm using it to put my currently selected candidate in the *Completions* 
buffer in the kill ring for further usage.

It's handy when hacking Elisp:
You can use describe-variable, function, face, you name it;
use the completions framework to search for your candidate;
and then put the selected candidate in the kill ring.

All the magic in the attached video is a simple interactive function 
that implements this workflow.

Thanks, /PA

> I'm not sure it's accurate to say they have done themselves harm
