> opportunity - and that is probably why I see an obligation for 
> myself to point it out.

"Obligation to point it out", sure.  But that's a far cry form
forbidding them to do that if they insist, or stopping to receive
patches from them because they do.

And please note that even the Bash example is not necessarily
relevant, because this mailing list is not about using Bash.  So
people who expect to see such trivial advice about Bash here have
wrong expectations.  Similarly with stuff only remotely related to
Emacs development, or not at all.  How to use LLMs wisely is such a
topic.

> >>> The stance that "we know better what's good for you" is IMO a 
> >>> disservice to our users.  I hope GNU will never go there.  If 
> >>> it ever does, I'll be outta here, given some firsthand 
> >>> experience I have with such regimes.
> >>
> >> I have a lot of sympathy for that, and I'm no fan of 
> >> paternalism  (or worse), but I'm convinced there is such a 
> >> thing as leadership  that doesn't fall afoul of the kinds of 
> >> concerns you describe.
> >
> > Cannot agree more, but where's the evidence that we don't 
> > provide exactly such kind of leadership?
> 
> You absolutely do provide leadership on matters you believe to be 
> relevant to Emacs.
> 
> So I think this debate is about relevance. For example we can 
> agree that various forms of deliberate "self-harm" by some users 
> is not relevant. (That's a weird example but I hope it makes 
> sense.)
> 
> But I think the lost opportunity to learn elisp by instead 
> favouring LLM use is less clear. In my experience learning elisp 
> is a large and invaluable part of the Emacs experience, and I say 
> that as someone who avoided learning elisp for the first 5 years 
> of my own use. The fact I now regard that as a great shame is a 
> large part of why I'm now arguing against LLMs.

People who want to submit changes without learning ELisp will soon
enough get negative feedback from us, whose purpose, among others, it
to lead them towards learning.  So I don't think I see the problem in
this part of our leadership.  I certainly don't see how refusing to
accept patches from them (assuming the patches pass our multilevel QA)
is TRT.

> Date: Fri, 20 Nov 2026 13:05:04 +0100
> From: "Pedro A. Aranda" <paaguti@gmail.com>
> Cc: emacs-devel@gnu.org
> 
> Attached is a first attempt at including move-lines-up and 
> move-lines-down in misc.el.

Thanks, comments below.

> +** New functions 'move-lines-up' and 'move-lines-down'.
> +These functions move the current line or region up or down. When a
> +region is selected, it will be extended to full lines. These functions
> +don't use the kill ring.

The last sentence doesn't belong to NEWS.  Also, this entry doesn't
mention the fact that one can move the stuff by ARG lines.

> +(defun move-lines-up (arg beg end)
> +  "Move region or line ARG times up when ARG > 0 or down when ARG < 0.

"ARG times" is not the best way of putting this.  I'd use

  Move current line up ARG lines.
  ARG is the prefix numeric argument and defaults to 1.
  Negative values move down.

> +Use the current line when nothing is selected.

I'd rephrase:

  If region is active, move the lines in the region instead.

> +Move full lines: if the mark or the point are
                                   ^^^^^^^^^
"point", not "the point".

> +not at the beginning or end of line, extend the region
> +automatically.

"Extend the region" is misleading, because the region is not affected.
Instead, I'd say

  ... if the mark or point are not at the beginning or end of a line,
  move the line(s) which include the mark and point positions.

> +    (let ((deactivate-mark nil)
> +          ;; Store the column when moving just one line
> +          (curcol (and (not (use-region-p)) (current-column))))

AFAIU, this comment is inaccurate because the column will be recorded
when the region is not active, but ARG is non-zero.

And why not try preserving the column in that other case as well?

> +	(unless (= 0 (forward-line arg))
> +	  (signal (if (< arg 0)
> +                      'beginning-of-buffer
> +                    'end-of-buffer))))

So in this case we don't move anything?  Why not move what we can
instead?

Thanks again for working on this.

Eli Zaretskii <eliz@gnu.org> writes:

>> >> Or do you mean that no LLM-generated code can pass the QA?
>> >
>> > I don't know.  If it does, why should we the Emacs developers care?
>>=20
>> Because if it does, then the feedback given to people who use an LLM
>> does not lead to learning, voiding one of the purposes of the feedback.
>
> Once again, it is not our responsibility to force contributors to
> learn.  No one should expect that from us.  OTOH, we shouldn't avoid
> providing the feedback due to suspicions that it will not be used.

That isn=E2=80=99t the point I wanted to make. The point is that by stating=
 as a
project that LLM-generated code is not accepted, the problem that
feedback doesn=E2=80=99t reach a person is much less likely.

Feeding feedback into an LLM is a problem, because if people do that
it=E2=80=99s so corrosive that even a friend of mine who took a deep dive i=
nto
agentic AI and has been using it to build software for production for
over a year now said that he stops working together with someone who
just feeds his reviews into a machine and sends the generated answers.

I know that=E2=80=99s an anecdote. Here=E2=80=99s some actual research on t=
he topic:
https://arxiv.org/html/2603.27249v2#S4

Best wishes,
Arne

probability that Emacs will soon die similar death?  If not, why not?

Thanks for looking into this. Attached is a new version of the patch.

On 20/11/26 13:25, Eli Zaretskii wrote:
>> Date: Fri, 20 Nov 2026 13:05:04 +0100
>> From: "Pedro A. Aranda" <paaguti@gmail.com>
>> Cc: emacs-devel@gnu.org
>>
>> Attached is a first attempt at including move-lines-up and
>> move-lines-down in misc.el.
> 
> Thanks, comments below.
> 
>> +** New functions 'move-lines-up' and 'move-lines-down'.
>> +These functions move the current line or region up or down. When a
>> +region is selected, it will be extended to full lines. These functions
>> +don't use the kill ring.
> 
> The last sentence doesn't belong to NEWS.  Also, this entry doesn't
> mention the fact that one can move the stuff by ARG lines.

Fixed.
>> +(defun move-lines-up (arg beg end)
>> +  "Move region or line ARG times up when ARG > 0 or down when ARG < 0.
> 
> "ARG times" is not the best way of putting this.  I'd use
> 
>    Move current line up ARG lines.
>    ARG is the prefix numeric argument and defaults to 1.
>    Negative values move down.
> 
>> +Use the current line when nothing is selected.
> 
> I'd rephrase:
> 
>    If region is active, move the lines in the region instead.
> 
>> +Move full lines: if the mark or the point are
>                                     ^^^^^^^^^
> "point", not "the point".
> 
>> +not at the beginning or end of line, extend the region
>> +automatically.
> 
> "Extend the region" is misleading, because the region is not affected.
> Instead, I'd say
> 
>    ... if the mark or point are not at the beginning or end of a line,
>    move the line(s) which include the mark and point positions.

I've rephrased the docstring completely.

>> +    (let ((deactivate-mark nil)
>> +          ;; Store the column when moving just one line
>> +          (curcol (and (not (use-region-p)) (current-column))))>
> AFAIU, this comment is inaccurate because the column will be recorded
> when the region is not active, but ARG is non-zero.

No, it says precisely what it does. I'm moving one line (the current 
line) when the region is not active and that's when I want to preserve 
the current column.
> And why not try preserving the column in that other case as well?

When selecting several lines, I would normally be working somewhere 
inside the region I move, while when I move just one line, it's more 
likely that I want to continue where I left it before moving the line.
  >> +	(unless (= 0 (forward-line arg))
>> +	  (signal (if (< arg 0)
>> +                      'beginning-of-buffer
>> +                    'end-of-buffer))))
> 
> So in this case we don't move anything?  Why not move what we can
> instead?

I don't use these functions programmatically, but I would, I'd rather 
stop a function from moving text beyond the limits of the buffer, 
because that is a sign that it is not calculating things correctly (IMHO).

> Thanks again for working on this.

Nest, /PA

>> > Btw, it seems there's a way to start the speedbar window display by
>> > invoking speedbar-window-mode interactively (as opposed to customizing
>> > speedbar-prefer-window and invoking "M-x speedbar").  The problem with
>> > that is that speedbar-prefer-window is left at its default nil value,
>> > so all kinds of bindings specific to this variant of Speedbar are not
>> > done.  Vincenzo, can we fix that, please?
>> 
>> I'm not quite sure how to do this. In the docstring for 'speedbar-mode', 
>> there's "\\{speedbar-mode-map}", which is always different from what 
>> 'describe-binding' returns because some of the key bindings are dynamic.
>> See 'speedbar-reconfigure-keymaps'.
>
> Maybe Stefan (CC'ed) could help here.

I'm not very familiar with `speedbar.el`, but based on a quick look at
`speedbar-reconfigure-keymaps` I think we have two options:

- Write the bindings "by hand" in the docstring (along with explanation
  about when which binding can be used) instead of relying on
  `\{speedbar-mode-map}`.
  That's upfront work and more maintenance work to keep it up-to-date
  when the code is changed.

- Try and get rid of `speedbar-reconfigure-keymaps`, maybe by relying on
  `:filter` to "statically" describe the dynamic part of the keymap and by creating
  two separate derived modes (one for the "frame" case and another for
  the "window" case).

Also in that function, I can't see why we do such a complicated dance
to compute `localmap`.  Would the patch below be correct, or are there
cases where the buffer of the frame we end up selecting is not
`speedbar-buffer` (or do we really want to run
`dframe-after-select-attached-frame-hook` here)?


=== Stefan

That's a tangent not relevant to the point I was making above.  But
since you bring this up: there are some people on our lists with whom
I prefer not to talk, but I do, because they contribute to Emacs.  I'm
sure every one of us has these experiences, where our personal
preferences take a back seat to our duties as Emacs maintainers and
developers.

conclusions of an academic paper which is based on researching other
projects are necessarily valid for us.

will be able to deal with these effects.  Assuming the legal issues

cannot deal with that without sacrificing something important.

I think there is a bug in the policy that decides when to start a
collection.  It sometimes seems to start a collection for every
allocation even if there is plenty of room left.  At that point
everything becomes very slow.  Maybe that's the case here and test does
not actually hang, it's just very slow.  It think the tests that
allocate very large objects can trigger that bug.  On Linux, I can use

   ulimit -S -d $((1024 * 1024 * 4))

to make the "largest" tests complete faster.  Is there something like
ulimit for MS-Windows?

"automatic memory compression" feature or whatever it's called.  The
large objects contain only zeros and presumably can be compressed very
well.  There the tests also become very slow even though one can
allocate huge objects.
